tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

content.content:
"""Exact, synthetic checks for judgment-to-controller feedback.

Nothing in this module calls a model, trains a learner, or runs an improvement
loop.  It types the channel by which a judgment reaches the process that
produces the next controller, and keeps the resulting *readout gap* separate
from baseline gain, robust regret, discrimination gap, and exploitability.

Three access classes order that channel.  ``sealed`` returns nothing,
``score_only`` returns an aggregate count, ``item_level`` returns per-item
outcomes.  Each is a deterministic coarsening of the next, so the finite
data-processing inequality used for observation-only Hide applies to what the
loop can learn about its own failures.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction as Q
from itertools import product
from math import comb

from spiral_ln.evaluation_game_testbed import _pushforward, _tv

ACCESS_CLASSES = ("sealed", "score_only", "item_level")
ROLES = ("selection", "readout")
EVENT_KINDS = ("score_query", "item_feedback", "readout")


def access_kernel(access: str, items: int) -> dict[str, dict[str, Q]]:
    """Deterministic feedback kernel from per-item outcome records.

    A record is a string of ``0``/``1`` of length ``items``.  The kernel says
    what reaches the loop, not what the evaluator stores.
    """

    if access not in ACCESS_CLASSES:
        raise ValueError("unknown access class")
    if type(items) is not int or items < 1:
        raise ValueError("items must be a positive integer")
    kernel = {}
    for bits in product("01", repeat=items):
        record = "".join(bits)
        if access == "sealed":
            image = "sealed"
        elif access == "score_only":
            image = f"score={record.count('1')}"
        else:
            image = record
        kernel[record] = {image: Q(1)}
    return kernel


def access_order_fixture() -> dict[str, object]:
    """Two controllers with equal scores and different failures.

    Item-level feedback separates them completely; score-only feedback cannot
    separate them at all.  A second pair with different scores is separated by
    both, and no pair is separated through a sealed set.
    """

    same_score = ({"10": Q(1)}, {"01": Q(1)})
    different_score = ({"11": Q(1)}, {"00": Q(1)})
    gaps = {}
    for name, (left, right) in (("same_score", same_score),
                                ("different_score", different_score)):
        gaps[name] = {
            access: _tv(_pushforward(left, access_kernel(access, 2)),
                        _pushforward(right, access_kernel(access, 2)))
            for access in ACCESS_CLASSES
        }
    ordered = all(g["sealed"] <= g["score_only"] <= g["item_level"] for g in gaps.values())
    return {"operator_type": "judgment_to_controller_feedback_kernel",
            "gaps": gaps, "access_classes_ordered_by_coarsening": ordered,
            "acts_between_generations": True, "changes_recorded_evidence": False}


def _binomial_pmf(n: int, p: Q) -> list[Q]:
    return [Q(comb(n, j)) * p**j * (1 - p)**(n - j) for j in range(n + 1)]


def selection_inflation(items: int, candidates: int, p: Q) -> dict[str, Q]:
    """Exact one-generation over-report from keeping the best-scoring candidate.

    Every candidate has the same true success probability ``p`` on each of
    ``items`` independent selection items, and candidates are independent.  The
    reported value is the selected candidate's score on those same items; the
    readout value is its expected score on untouched items, which is ``p``.
    This isolates the selection term.  It says nothing about real gains,
    persistence across generations, or correlated candidates.
    """

    if type(items) is not int or type(candidates) is not int or items < 1 or candidates < 1:
        raise ValueError("items and candidates must be positive integers")
    if not 0 <= p <= 1:
        raise ValueError("p must be a probability")
    pmf = _binomial_pmf(items, p)
    cumulative, running = [], Q(0)
    for mass in pmf:
        running += mass
        cumulative.append(running)
    expected_max = sum(
        j * (cumulative[j]**candidates - (cumulative[j - 1]**candidates if j else Q(0)))
        for j in range(items + 1)
    )
    reported = expected_max / items
    return {"expected_reported": reported, "readout_value": p,
            "readout_gap": reported - p}


def observed_accuracy(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q) -> Q:
    """Accuracy against observed labels when labels flip independently."""

    if not 0 <= clean_accuracy <= 1 or not 0 <= flip <= 1:
        raise ValueError("probabilities required")
    return clean_accuracy * (1 - flip) + (1 - clean_accuracy) * flip


def noise_ceiling(flip: Q) -> Q:
    """Best observed-label accuracy available to a predictor that cannot see
    which labels flipped."""

    if not 0 <= flip <= 1:
        raise ValueError("flip must be a probability")
    return max(flip, 1 - flip)


def memorized_selection_score(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q, patch_share: Q) -> Q:
    """Selection-set score after memorizing a share of its observed labels.

    The memorized items are chosen independently of whether the controller
    already got them right, so the remainder keep the base observed accuracy.
    Memorized items score one.  Collateral effects of a patch on other items
    are assumed absent, which a real learner need not satisfy.
    """

    if not 0 <= patch_share <= 1:
        raise ValueError("patch share must lie in [0, 1]")
    base = observed_accuracy(clean_accuracy, flip)
    return patch_share + (1 - patch_share) * base


def targeted_patch_selection_score(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q, patch_share: Q) -> Q:
    """Selection-set score after memorizing failed items only.

    This is what item-level feedback supplies: each patch turns one failed
    item into a pass and leaves every other item unchanged.  ``patch_share``
    is measured against the whole set and cannot exceed the failure share.
    """

    base = observed_accuracy(clean_accuracy, flip)
    if not 0 <= patch_share <= 1 - base:
        raise ValueError("patch share must lie between zero and the failure share")
    return base + patch_share


def ceiling_detection_threshold(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q) -> Q:
    """Share of the set, memorized independently of outcomes, above which the
    selection score exceeds the noise ceiling.

    Below this share the ceiling check is silent however much was memorized.
    """

    base = observed_accuracy(clean_accuracy, flip)
    if base >= 1:
        raise ValueError("base observed accuracy must be below one")
    return max(Q(0), (noise_ceiling(flip) - base) / (1 - base))


def targeted_ceiling_detection_threshold(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q) -> Q:
    """Share of the set, patched on failed items only, above which the
    selection score exceeds the noise ceiling.

    As a share of the failed items this equals ``ceiling_detection_threshold``;
    as a share of the set it is smaller by the failure share.
    """

    base = observed_accuracy(clean_accuracy, flip)
    if base >= 1:
        raise ValueError("base observed accuracy must be below one")
    return max(Q(0), noise_ceiling(flip) - base)


def failed_item_noise_share(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q) -> Q:
    """Probability that an item the base predictor fails has a flipped label.

    The predictor errs on the clean label independently of the flip.  It fails
    the observed label either by being right about a flipped item or wrong
    about an unflipped one.
    """

    wrong_because_flipped = flip * clean_accuracy
    wrong_unflipped = (1 - flip) * (1 - clean_accuracy)
    if wrong_because_flipped + wrong_unflipped == 0:
        raise ValueError("the predictor never fails an observed label")
    return wrong_because_flipped / (wrong_because_flipped + wrong_unflipped)


def noise_ceiling_fixture() -> dict[str, Q]:
    clean, flip = Q(4, 5), Q(1, 10)
    base = observed_accuracy(clean, flip)
    targeted = targeted_ceiling_detection_threshold(clean, flip)
    return {
        "clean_accuracy": clean, "flip_probability": flip,
        "base_observed_accuracy": base,
        "noise_ceiling": noise_ceiling(flip),
        "score_half_memorized": memorized_selection_score(clean, flip, Q(1, 2)),
        "score_fully_memorized": memorized_selection_score(clean, flip, Q(1)),
        "ceiling_detection_threshold": ceiling_detection_threshold(clean, flip),
        "targeted_threshold_share_of_set": targeted,
        "targeted_threshold_share_of_failures": targeted / (1 - base),
        "score_all_failures_patched": targeted_patch_selection_score(clean, flip, 1 - base),
        "failed_item_noise_share": failed_item_noise_share(clean, flip),
    }


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EvalSet:
    set_id: str
    role: str
    access: str
    item_ids: tuple[str, ...]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class LoopEvent:
    generation: int
    set_id: str
    kind: str
    item_ids: tuple[str, ...] = ()


def audit_ledger(sets, events, readout_budget, exhaustion_bound):
    """Check a multi-generation feedback ledger against its declarations.

    Malformed declarations raise.  Breaches of a well-formed declaration are
    recorded, and move the affected endpoint to ``not_evaluated``, because a
    breach is a finding about the run and should survive into its report.

    A ``score_query`` or ``item_feedback`` event means the result reached the
    loop.  A ``readout`` event means the experimenter read a sealed set; if a
    loop-affecting decision followed, that reading is itself adaptive, so the
    number of readouts is budgeted.  Identifiers detect recorded overlap only.
    They cannot certify that two differently named items are independent.
    """

    if not sets:
        raise ValueError("at least one evaluation set must be declared")
    if type(readout_budget) is not int or readout_budget < 1:
        raise ValueError("readout budget must be a positive integer")
    if not exhaustion_bound > 0:
        raise ValueError("exhaustion bound must be positive")
    declared, owner = {}, {}
    for item in sets:
        if (not item.set_id or item.role not in ROLES or item.access not in ACCESS_CLASSES
                or not item.item_ids or len(set(item.item_ids)) != len(item.item_ids)):
            raise ValueError("invalid evaluation set declaration")
        if item.set_id in declared:
            raise ValueError("duplicate set identifier")
        if item.role == "readout" and item.access != "sealed":
            raise ValueError("a readout set must be declared sealed")
        for identifier in item.item_ids:
            if identifier in owner:
                raise ValueError("selection/readout identifiers overlap")
            owner[identifier] = item.set_id
        declared[item.set_id] = item
    if not any(item.role == "readout" for item in sets):
        raise ValueError("no readout set declared")

    state = {
        set_id: {"role": item.role, "declared_access": item.access,
                 "size": len(item.item_ids), "score_queries": 0, "patches": 0,
                 "distinct_patched": set(), "readouts": [], "retired_at": None,
                 "breaches": []}
        for set_id, item in declared.items()
    }
    previous = None
    for event in events:
        if (type(event.generation) is not int or event.generation < 0
                or event.kind not in EVENT_KINDS or event.set_id not in declared):
            raise ValueError("invalid loop event")
        if previous is not None and event.generation < previous:
            raise ValueError("events must be ordered by generation")
        previous = event.generation
        target, record = declared[event.set_id], state[event.set_id]
        if event.kind == "readout":
            if target.role != "readout":
                raise ValueError("readout events apply to readout sets only")
            record["readouts"].append(event.generation)
            if len(record["readouts"]) > readout_budget:
                record["breaches"].append(f"readout budget exceeded at generation {event.generation}")
            continue
        if event.kind == "item_feedback":
            if not event.item_ids or not set(event.item_ids) <= set(target.item_ids):
                raise ValueError("item feedback must name items of its own set")
        if target.role == "readout":
            record["breaches"].append(
                f"{event.kind} exposed the readout set at generation {event.generation}")
            continue
        if record["retired_at"] is not None:
            record["breaches"].append(f"used after retirement at generation {event.generation}")
        allowed = ACCESS_CLASSES.index(target.access)
        needed = ACCESS_CLASSES.index("item_level" if event.kind == "item_feedback" else "score_only")
        if needed > allowed:
            record["breaches"].append(
                f"{event.kind} exceeds declared {target.access} access at generation {event.generation}")
        if event.kind == "score_query":
            record["score_queries"] += 1
        else:
            record["patches"] += len(event.item_ids)
            record["distinct_patched"].update(event.item_ids)
            if (record["retired_at"] is None
                    and Q(record["patches"], record["size"]) > exhaustion_bound):
                record["retired_at"] = event.generation

    report = {"selection": {}, "readout": {},
              "identifier_scope": "recorded overlap only; independence is not certified"}
    for set_id, record in state.items():
        if record["role"] == "selection":
            report["selection"][set_id] = {
                "declared_access": record["declared_access"], "size": record["size"],
                "score_queries": record["score_queries"], "patches": record["patches"],
                "distinct_patched": len(record["distinct_patched"]),
                "patch_share": Q(record["patches"], record["size"]),
                "retired_at_generation": record["retired_at"],
                "breaches": tuple(record["breaches"]),
                "selection_scores_usable_as_endpoints": False,
            }
        else:
            report["readout"][set_id] = {
                "size": record["size"], "readouts": len(record["readouts"]),
                "readout_generations": tuple(record["readouts"]),
                "breaches": tuple(record["breaches"]),
                "endpoint_status": "not_evaluated" if record["breaches"] else "evaluable",
            }
    report["declarations_respected"] = not any(
        entry["breaches"] for group in ("selection", "readout")
        for entry in report[group].values())
    return report


def divergence_flags(points, margin):
    """Compare selection-set and readout-set gains between permitted readouts.

    ``points`` are ``(generation, selection_score, readout_score)`` at strictly
    increasing generations.  A flag voids claims resting on the selection set.
    It does not void the sealed readout.
    """

    points = list(points)
    if len(points) < 2:
        raise ValueError("at least two readout points required")
    if not margin >= 0:
        raise ValueError("margin must be nonnegative")
    rows = []
    for (g0, s0, r0), (g1, s1, r1) in zip(points, points[1:]):
        if type(g0) is not int or type(g1) is not int or g1 <= g0:
            raise ValueError("generations must be strictly increasing integers")
        if not all(0 <= value <= 1 for value in (s0, r0, s1, r1)):
            raise ValueError("scores must lie in [0, 1]")
        divergence = (s1 - s0) - (r1 - r0)
        rows.append({"from_generation": g0, "to_generation": g1,
                     "selection_gain": s1 - s0, "readout_gain": r1 - r0,
                     "divergence": divergence, "readout_gap_at_end": s1 - r1,
                     "flagged": divergence > margin})
    return rows


def run_ledger_fixture() -> dict[str, object]:
    """One respected ledger and one breached ledger over the same declarations."""

    selection = EvalSet("S", "selection", "score_only", tuple(f"s{i}" for i in range(8)))
    readout = EvalSet("R", "readout", "sealed", tuple(f"r{i}" for i in range(8)))
    clean_events = (
        LoopEvent(0, "R", "readout"),
        LoopEvent(1, "S", "score_query"), LoopEvent(1, "S", "score_query"),
        LoopEvent(2, "S", "score_query"), LoopEvent(2, "R", "readout"),
    )
    breached_events = clean_events + (
        LoopEvent(3, "S", "item_feedback", ("s0", "s1")),
        LoopEvent(4, "R", "score_query"),
    )
    return {"respected": audit_ledger((selection, readout), clean_events, 3, Q(1, 2)),
            "breached": audit_ledger((selection, readout), breached_events, 3, Q(1, 2))}


def verify() -> dict[str, object]:
    """Run all exact fixtures and return machine-readable checks."""

    order = access_order_fixture()
    smallest = selection_inflation(1, 2, Q(1, 2))
    ladder = {n: selection_inflation(n, 2, Q(1, 2))["readout_gap"] for n in (1, 4, 16, 64)}
    widening = {k: selection_inflation(4, k, Q(1, 2))["readout_gap"] for k in (1, 2, 4, 16)}
    noise = noise_ceiling_fixture()
    ledgers = run_ledger_fixture()
    flags = divergence_flags(((0, Q(7, 10), Q(7, 10)), (50, Q(4, 5), Q(37, 50)),
                              (100, Q(83, 100), Q(73, 100))), Q(1, 50))
    checks = {
        "item_level_separates_equal_scores_and_score_only_does_not":
            order["gaps"]["same_score"] == {"sealed": Q(0), "score_only": Q(0), "item_level": Q(1)},
        "access_classes_ordered": order["access_classes_ordered_by_coarsening"],
        "two_candidates_one_item_gap_is_quarter": smallest["readout_gap"] == Q(1, 4),
        "single_candidate_has_no_selection_gap": widening[1] == 0,
        "selection_gap_shrinks_with_items": ladder[1] > ladder[4] > ladder[16] > ladder[64] > 0,
        "selection_gap_grows_with_candidates": widening[1] < widening[2] < widening[4] < widening[16],
        "full_memorization_exceeds_noise_ceiling":
            noise["score_fully_memorized"] == 1 > noise["noise_ceiling"],
        "half_memorization_stays_below_ceiling":
            noise["score_half_memorized"] < noise["noise_ceiling"],
        "ceiling_check_threshold_is_eight_thirteenths":
            noise["ceiling_detection_threshold"] == Q(8, 13),
        "targeted_patching_crosses_at_four_twentyfifths_of_set":
            noise["targeted_threshold_share_of_set"] == Q(4, 25)
            and noise["targeted_threshold_share_of_failures"] == noise["ceiling_detection_threshold"],
        "failed_items_enriched_for_flipped_labels":
            noise["failed_item_noise_share"] == Q(4, 13) > noise["flip_probability"],
        "respected_ledger_leaves_readout_evaluable":
            ledgers["respected"]["declarations_respected"]
            and ledgers["respected"]["readout"]["R"]["endpoint_status"] == "evaluable",
        "breached_ledger_withholds_endpoint":
            ledgers["breached"]["readout"]["R"]["endpoint_status"] == "not_evaluated"
            and bool(ledgers["breached"]["selection"]["S"]["breaches"]),
        "selection_scores_never_endpoints":
            not ledgers["respected"]["selection"]["S"]["selection_scores_usable_as_endpoints"],
        "divergence_flags_fire_when_selection_outruns_readout":
            [row["flagged"] for row in flags] == [True, True]
            and flags[1]["readout_gain"] < 0 < flags[1]["selection_gain"],
    }
    return {"evidence_status": "exact_synthetic_fixtures_not_model_or_agent_evidence",
            "checks": checks, "all_passed": all(checks.values()),
            "access_order": order,
            "selection_inflation": {"one_item_two_candidates": smallest,
                                    "gap_by_items_two_candidates": ladder,
                                    "gap_by_candidates_four_items": widening},
            "noise_ceiling": noise, "ledger": ledgers, "divergence": flags}

# Feedback channel: suggested insertions for the evaluation design calculus

Draft 0.2 — 2026-10-12. Suggestions only. Draft 0.2 states the ceiling law for
failure-targeted patching as well as for patching chosen at random.

This file changes nothing in `evaluation_design_calculus.md` or
`evaluation_game_testbed.md`. Each block names a location in those documents,
offers text for it, and states what supports the text. Where a block is adopted,
its wording should be made the author's own. Where it is not, the executable
fixtures still stand by themselves.

The gap being addressed: the calculus already says that a judgment "shown during
play or used for learning ... also enters observations or controller updates"
(§2), and that frozen-controller sensitivity differs from sensitivity "after
retraining, selecting another controller" (§7). It has no operator for that
channel, no estimand for what the channel does to a score, and no record of how
often it was used. A self-improvement loop is that channel applied once per
generation.

## Evidence behind the suggestions

| Level | Source | What it supplies |
|---|---|---|
| Finite verified example | `src/spiral_ln/evaluation_game_feedback.py`, 30 tests, receipt under `output/evaluation_game_feedback/` | Access-class ordering, one-generation selection gap, noise-ceiling threshold, failed-item enrichment, ledger enforcement |
| Synthetic mechanism result | `output/eval_reuse_toys/` (two seeded simulations, predictions hashed before each run) | Multi-generation behaviour of the gap under score-only and item-level feedback |
| Not available | — | Any language-model loop, any observed controller |

The simulations are JavaScript, seeded, and not exact. Their prediction record
is 5 of 6 in the first run and 3 of 6 in the second, and both overpredicted the
size of the gap. One arm of the second run was added after its sealed results
were seen and is marked exploratory in its own files.

## A. §2, after "Maintain three distinctions"

Suggested fourth distinction:

> 4. A judgment that reaches whatever produces the next controller is a channel.
> Its source set, its access class, and the number of times it was used belong
> in the experiment record. A score measured on a set that fed this channel is a
> selection score. A capability claim needs a set that did not.

## B. §3, operator table

Suggested row:

| Proposed operator | Primary effect | Required detail |
|---|---|---|
| \(\operatorname{Feedback}_{s,q}\) | Controller roster/protocol of a later generation | Source set \(s\); access class \(q\in\{\text{sealed},\text{score-only},\text{item-level}\}\); whether the consumer selects among candidates or supplies a training input; generation scope. |

Suggested sentence beneath the table:

> Feedback is not \(\operatorname{Rescore}\), which is offline, and not
> \(\operatorname{Observe}\), which changes what the evaluator records. It reads
> \(J\) restricted to \(s\) and writes \(\Pi\) for the next generation. Declaring
> a set sealed while a score from it reaches the loop is ill-typed.

## C. §4, after the sentence on `Repeat` and reset/carry maps

> Generations joined by Feedback are not independent blocks. The carry map
> carries the controller, and with it whatever of \(s\) the channel transmitted.
> Aggregating a per-generation score across such generations as if each were a
> fresh draw of the same experiment mistakes the unit.

## D. §5, three laws and one observation

**Coarsening law.**

> The access classes are ordered: sealed is a deterministic function of the
> score, and the score is a deterministic function of the per-item outcomes.
> Total-variation distance between two controllers' feedback therefore cannot
> increase from item-level to score-only to sealed. Two controllers that fail
> different items with equal totals are separated completely by item-level
> feedback and not at all by a score.

Support: `access_order_fixture`; the ordering is checked for every pair of
distributions on a rational grid over two-item outcomes.

**Selection law.**

> Keeping the best of \(K\) candidates by score on \(s\), then reporting that
> score, overstates: \(\mathbb E[\max_k\hat S_k]\ge\max_k\mathbb E[\hat S_k]\).
> This is the same convexity as the mixture law, with the candidate index in
> place of the mixture component. For candidates of equal true value
> one half, two candidates and one item give a reported value of three quarters.

Support: `selection_inflation`, checked against independent enumeration of
every outcome matrix in seven small cells. Exact gaps for two candidates at
\(p=\tfrac12\) are \(\tfrac14\), \(\tfrac{35}{256}\), about 0.0700 and about
0.0352 at 1, 4, 16 and 64 items; multiplied by \(\sqrt n\) these are 0.250,
0.273, 0.280 and 0.282. The value \(1/(2\sqrt\pi)\approx0.2821\) is the
standard Gaussian figure for the larger of two draws. The fixture verifies the
listed cells and no limit.

Boundary: one generation, equal candidates, independent items. Accumulation
across generations is a simulation result, not an exact one.

**Ceiling law.**

> With labels flipped independently at rate \(\varepsilon<\tfrac12\), no
> predictor blind to the flips exceeds \(1-\varepsilon\) in expectation on
> observed labels. Let \(v\) be the controller's observed accuracy before any
> item of \(s\) is memorized. If it memorizes a share \(m/n\) of \(s\) chosen
> without regard to its outcomes, it scores \(m/n+(1-m/n)v\) on \(s\) and
> crosses the ceiling only when \(m/n>(1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\). If it memorizes
> items it failed, which is what item-level feedback supplies, it scores
> \(v+m/n\) and crosses when \(m/n>1-\varepsilon-v\): the same threshold
> \((1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\), now as a share of the failed items. Below the
> threshold a ceiling check is silent.

Support: `ceiling_detection_threshold` and
`targeted_ceiling_detection_threshold`. With clean accuracy \(\tfrac45\) and
\(\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}\): \(v=\tfrac{37}{50}\). Memorizing at random, the
check is silent below \(\tfrac8{13}\) of the set. Patching failures, it is
silent below \(\tfrac4{25}\) of the set, which is \(\tfrac8{13}\) of the failed
items. Both formulas assume a memorized item has no effect on any other item.
The nearest-neighbour learner in the second simulation did not satisfy that,
and it also did not reliably absorb a patch: at \(n=4000\) it patched a quarter
of the set and its reported score stayed at 0.759, below the 0.90 ceiling.

**Observation on what item-level feedback selects.**

> An item the controller fails is more likely than an average item to carry a
> wrong label, whenever the controller is better than chance:
> \(\Pr[\text{flipped}\mid\text{failed}]=\varepsilon a/(\varepsilon a+(1-\varepsilon)(1-a))\),
> which exceeds \(\varepsilon\) exactly when \(a>\tfrac12\). Feeding failures
> back concentrates label noise in what the next controller is built from.

Support: `failed_item_noise_share`; \(\tfrac4{13}\) against a base rate of
\(\tfrac1{10}\) in the fixture. In the second simulation the measured share
among patched items was 20–29% against the same 10% base rate. This is the
reason the unchecked answer in the Proposer–Solver recipe (atlas §11) matters
once its output is fed back.

Suggested closing sentence, matching the section's existing last line:

> No unconditional claim is made that feedback lowers readout performance. In
> the simulations, score-only selection of fresh training batches raised it.

## E. §7, after the definition of the order effect

> For a controller \(\pi_g\) produced with feedback from \(s\), and a sealed set
> \(r\) from the same sampling law, define the readout gap
> \(\rho_g=V^{s}_{\pi_g}-V^{r}_{\pi_g}\). It compares two measurements of one
> controller, not two designs, so it is not a design difference. A gain series
> computed on \(s\) estimates the change in value plus the change in \(\rho\).

## F. §11, the evaluation card

Suggested amendment to item 6:

> ... and whether any score feeds back into play *or into the production of a
> later controller*.

Suggested additional item:

> 10. **Feedback ledger:** for each evaluation set, its role (selection or
> readout), declared access class, score queries, items fed back, number and
> generation of readouts, and the rule that retires it.

## G. `evaluation_game_testbed.md`, estimand table

Suggested fifth row:

| Estimand | Definition | It is not |
|---|---|---|
| Readout gap | \(\rho=V^{s}_\pi-V^{r}_\pi\), with \(s\) having fed judgment to the loop and \(r\) sealed | A baseline gain, or evidence that capability changed |

Suggested section, placed after "Executable confirmation and adversarial
checks":

> ### Feedback channel and multi-generation ledger
>
> `evaluation_game_feedback.py` extends the single split enforced by `confirm()`
> to a sequence of generations. Sets are declared with a role and an access
> class. Events record a score reaching the loop, items reaching the loop, or an
> experimenter reading a sealed set. Malformed declarations and malformed
> events raise: a readout set not declared sealed, identifiers shared across
> sets, or a readout event naming a selection set (a readout is by definition
> a read of a sealed set; a selection set is read through score queries).
> Breaches of a well-formed declaration are recorded instead, and move the
> readout endpoint to `not_evaluated`: a breach is a finding about the run.
> A sealed read transmits nothing and is not an event, so `Feedback` at sealed
> access is always well-typed. The [composition note](evaluation_feedback_composition.md)
> checks that, under these rules, well-typed sequences are exactly those the
> ledger reports as respected, on every sequence of length at most four over a
> nine-operator alphabet. Reads of the
> sealed set are budgeted, since a stop-or-continue decision taken on a readout
> is itself adaptive. Identifiers detect recorded overlap. They do not certify
> independence.
>
> ```powershell
> $env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
> python scripts/verify_evaluation_game_feedback.py --output output/evaluation_game_feedback/feedback_v0_2.json
> python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_game_feedback.py -q
> ```

## H. What is not delivered

- `Feedback` is not implemented against `hive_lab` adapters or any external
  policy. The module checks declarations and arithmetic.
- No loop with a language model has been run. The first observed-controller
  study would pair a small model with a declared selection set and a sealed
  readout, and report the ledger.
- Partial leakage, where the loop learns failure categories and not items, is
  now treated in [evaluation_feedback_lattice.md](evaluation_feedback_lattice.md):
  category channels form a lattice of partial leaks, with the cost of each
  position exact. Composition with the other operators is in
  [evaluation_feedback_composition.md](evaluation_feedback_composition.md),
  and the selection gap across generations in
  [evaluation_feedback_multigen.md](evaluation_feedback_multigen.md).
- The simulations fix one parameter set each. No sweep over candidate count,
  decay rate, or label-noise rate was run.

## 11. A reusable evaluation card

Every design should declare:

1. **Claim and population:** the behavior being tested and where the conclusion is intended to apply.
2. **Game and primitives:** state, legal actions, transitions, resource ledgers, observation channels, utilities, stopping, and presentation.
3. **Controllers:** focal policy, counterparts, memory, prompts, tools, budgets, and any learning or selection between episodes.
4. **Design expression:** ordered, scoped operators with preconditions, footprints, and preservation obligations.
5. **Reference model:** fixed-policy baseline, optimal decision rule, Nash/Bayesian/sequential reference, or an explicitly heuristic comparator.
6. **Acquisition and judgment:** privileged versus accessible data, blind scoring where relevant, and whether any score feeds back into play.
7. **Estimand:** main effect, interaction, order effect, frontier, calibration error, welfare, or unilateral-improvement gap.
8. **Inference:** assignment, independent blocks, frozen selection/confirmation boundary, uncertainty, and multiplicity.
9. **Evidence status:** algebraic identity, finite verified example, synthetic mechanism result, observed-controller result, or externally validated claim.

The first implementation priority would be compiling these cards against real adapters and checking observation boundaries. A full game-language compiler, open-game strategic semantics, and real-model campaigns are subsequent goals, not results delivered by this document.

## 1. Channels are partitions; the lattice data-processing law

A deterministic feedback channel on records \(\{0,1\}^n\) is a function \(f\);
two channels carry the same information exactly when \(\ker f\) agrees, so a
channel *is* a partition of the record set. Convention: \(p\le q\) when \(q\)
refines \(p\); the one-block partition (`sealed`) is the bottom, the discrete
partition (`item_level`) the top, \(p\vee q\) the common refinement (observing
both) and \(p\wedge q\) the finest common coarsening (components of the union
of the two relations). This is the partition lattice, orientation reversed.

**Proposition 1 (lattice data-processing law and converse).** For all
distributions \(P,Q\) on records, \(p\le q\) implies
\(\mathrm{TV}(p_\#P,p_\#Q)\le\mathrm{TV}(q_\#P,q_\#Q)\); and if \(p\not\le q\)
there are point masses \(P,Q\) reversing the inequality.

*Proof.* \(\mathrm{TV}(p_\#P,p_\#Q)=\max_U|P(U)-Q(U)|\) over unions \(U\) of
blocks of \(p\). When \(q\) refines \(p\), every block of \(p\) is a union of
blocks of \(q\), so the maximum for \(p\) ranges over a subset of the sets
